name: Lattice energy
seoDesc: Lattice energy: work out your result from the stoichiometry and the closest interatomic distance. A free chemistry calculator with the formula, units and…
summary:
Supply the stoichiometry, the closest interatomic distance and the custom interatomic distance and the Lattice energy calculator solves for the answer. It is built for a bench calculation involving amounts, concentrations or reaction ratios.

Nothing is submitted anywhere: the arithmetic runs in the page you are looking at.

sections.title: How does the Lattice energy calculator work?
sections.html:
The Lattice energy calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationships described below and reports every result it can derive from them.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (the chosen approximation, the element (Cation) and the element (Anion)); then you type in the stoichiometry, the closest interatomic distance, the custom interatomic distance and the born-Landé repulsive contribution.

Press Calculate once and the page holds the relationship, tracking which boxes you filled and working out everything else; from that point on it follows every edit you make.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the Lattice energy calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

K=kapustinskii × (atomic radius + atomic radius) ÷ (kapustinskii's Born approximation × stoichiometry × the absolute value of (charge × charge))
Kapustinskii's Born approximation=(-D + atomic radius + atomic radius) ÷ (atomic radius + atomic radius)
Charge=-four pi epsilon × born-Landé × closest interatomic distance ÷ (madelung constant × na × born-Landé repulsive contribution × (qe ^ 2) × charge)
Born exponent (n)=-1 ÷ (born-Landé repulsive contribution − 1)
Charge=-four pi epsilon × born-Mayer × closest interatomic distance ÷ (madelung constant × na × born-Mayer repulsive contribution × (qe ^ 2) × charge)
Compressibility factor (ρ)=closest interatomic distance × (1 − born-Mayer repulsive contribution)

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Units are handled by conversion rather than by convention. Whatever chip you choose, the number is turned into a single base unit before the calculation and rendered back afterwards, so a form filled with a mixture of systems still gives the right answer.

Display rounding is separate from calculation rounding: the digits you see are shortened, the value behind them is not. Numbers far from everyday size are shown in scientific notation so the significant digits stay readable.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Lattice energy calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Working through a stoichiometry problem
  • Converting between the units a protocol and your bench equipment use
  • Preparing a solution and checking the numbers first
  • Any time the same 3 figures keep coming back — the stoichiometry, the closest interatomic distance and the custom interatomic distance — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.
  • Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.
  • Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.
  • Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Lattice energy calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the stoichiometry, the closest interatomic distance and the custom interatomic distance, which is 17 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter atomic radius (Cation) in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Atomic radius (Cation) opens in picometers and the chip beside it offers 34 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There are several choices to make (5 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Charge = 0. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Lattice energy calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
